questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: explain how polar covalent bonds make water a polar molecule
questions.stem: A student draws a water molecule as a bent shape with both hydrogen atoms crowded onto one side of the oxygen. What produces that shape and that charge distribution?

options.text: Oxygen draws the shared electrons away, leaving each hydrogen partially positive
Oxygen carries a full negative charge that repels both hydrogen nuclei
options.misconception: treats the polar bond as a complete transfer of electrons to oxygen

options.text: The two hydrogen nuclei repel each other and bend away from the oxygen atom
options.misconception: blames hydrogen-hydrogen repulsion instead of oxygen's lone pairs

options.text: Water is bent because its two bonds must point in opposite directions
options.misconception: believes any two-bonded molecule must be linear by necessity

questions.explanation: Oxygen has more valence electrons than hydrogen and pulls the shared pair in each O-H bond toward itself, so both bonds are polar covalent: oxygen ends up partially negative and each hydrogen partially positive. Two lone pairs on the oxygen squeeze the O-H bonds into a 104.5 degree bend, which is what concentrates the partial charges on one side of the molecule and lets water hydrogen-bond. The tempting belief that oxygen holds a full negative charge fails because the electrons are still shared, not transferred, so the molecule as a whole is neutral.
questions.hint: Ask which atom has the stronger pull on the shared electrons.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: relate hydrogen bonding between water molecules to surface tension
questions.stem: A pond skater stands on the surface of a still pond and its six legs dimple the water without sinking through. What holds the insect up?

options.text: Hydrogen bonds between water molecules that resist being pulled apart
A thin cushion of trapped air under the legs carrying the insect's weight
options.misconception: believes a trapped air film does all of the supporting

options.text: Static charge on the legs repelling the hydrogen bonds in the water
options.misconception: attributes support to static repulsion instead of surface tension

options.text: The legs pushing down while the water pressure pushes back upward
options.misconception: confuses surface tension with a rigid floor rebounding

questions.explanation: Water molecules hydrogen-bond to each other, and at the liquid surface those bonds are not replaced by neighbours on the far side, so the surface behaves like a stretched sheet that resists being pulled apart. A pond skater's weight per leg is far below the force needed to break that sheet, so the surface deforms into a dimple but holds. The tempting belief that the legs rest on trapped air fails because the insect holds on a clean surface too, and the water is not rebounding like a rigid floor, since the dimple shows it deforming.
questions.hint: Think about what happens to the bonds at a liquid surface.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: explain capillary rise by adhesion and cohesion together
questions.stem: A figure shows two straight glass tubes of the same height standing in a beaker of coloured water. In both tubes the water climbs above the beaker level and stops at a concave meniscus, and it climbs noticeably higher in the narrower tube. Which combination of interactions explains the taller column in the narrow tube?

options.text: Water adheres to the glass and coheres to itself, and the narrow tube amplifies it
Water dissolves some glass in the thin tube and rises inside the dissolved bubbles
options.misconception: believes glass dissolves and the climb is caused by rising bubbles

options.text: The thin tube holds warmer water that expands upward against gravity
options.misconception: attributes capillary rise to thermal expansion instead of surface forces

options.text: Air pressure pushing the column higher where the tube diameter is smaller
options.misconception: confuses capillary action with air pressure on a small area

questions.explanation: Capillary rise starts at the water-glass interface: polar water molecules hydrogen-bond to the charged silanol groups on the glass, so they are pulled up the wall, and because they also hydrogen-bond to each other they drag the rest of the column with them until gravity balances the upward pull of surface tension. The narrower the tube, the smaller the mass of water that has to be held up, so the column reaches higher. The tempting belief that air pressure does the lifting confuses this with a piston, and glass does not dissolve to make bubbles.
questions.hint: Two interactions act here: one is to the wall, one is to the water itself.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: explain why ice is less dense than liquid water
questions.stem: Ice cubes float at the surface of a glass of water instead of sinking to the bottom. Which fact about the structure of solid water explains this?

options.text: Ice locks hydrogens into an open lattice that spaces its molecules further apart
Ice is colder than liquid water, and anything cold always floats on warm
options.misconception: believes temperature alone sets buoyancy for every substance

options.text: Ice consists mostly of oxygen atoms, which are lighter than the hydrogen
options.misconception: misreads the water molecule as mostly oxygen with free hydrogen

options.text: Ice holds trapped air bubbles, and the trapped gas makes the cube buoyant
options.misconception: attributes flotation to dissolved air rather than lattice structure

questions.explanation: In ice every oxygen forms four hydrogen bonds in a roughly tetrahedral arrangement, and that geometry builds an open hexagonal lattice containing more empty space than liquid water has, so a given volume of ice holds fewer molecules and is less dense. The tempting belief that anything cold floats fails because a denser cold liquid still sinks through colder water, and the loss of some hydrogen bonds in the liquid is exactly what lets liquid molecules pack closer, so the open lattice must be the cause.
questions.hint: Count the bonds each oxygen makes in the two states.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: identify ion-dipole hydration of dissolved ions
questions.stem: A figure shows a sodium ion at the centre with eight water molecules arranged evenly around it, each water turned so its partially negative oxygen points toward the ion and its partially positive hydrogens point away. What is this arrangement called and what holds it together?

options.text: A hydration shell, held by ion-dipole attractions to the water oxygens
A hydration shell, held by covalent bonds from the ion to each oxygen
options.misconception: treats ion-water attraction as full covalent bonding

options.text: A protein coat, held by hydrogen bonds to folded amino acid side chains
options.misconception: confuses a water shell around an ion with a polypeptide

options.text: A micelle, held by hydrophobic tails turning away from the ion
options.misconception: confuses an ionic solution with a lipid micelle

questions.explanation: The picture shows a hydration shell: water is a polar molecule, so its partially negative oxygen is attracted to the sodium cation and its partially positive hydrogens point out toward the bulk solvent. The attraction is ion-dipole, an electrostatic interaction that water supports well because its high dielectric constant screens the charge, but it is not a covalent bond, so the shell keeps rearranging as water molecules swap places. The tempting belief that the shell is a protein confuses a solvent effect with a macromolecule, and a micelle forms from amphipathic lipids, not from water.
questions.hint: Name the interaction between a charged particle and a polar molecule.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Acids and Bases: pH from Hydrogen Ions
questions.learningObjective: compute a pH from a hydrogen ion concentration
questions.stem: A flask of gastric fluid is measured at a hydrogen ion concentration of 3.2 × 10⁻⁴ molar. What is the pH of that fluid, to two decimal places?

options.misconception: adds the mantissa to the exponent instead of subtracting it
reads the exponent as the pH without taking a logarithm
reports only the mantissa and discards the exponent

questions.explanation: pH is the negative base-ten logarithm of the hydrogen ion concentration, so pH equals negative log of 3.2 × 10⁻⁴, which is 4 minus log of 3.2, that is 4 minus 0.505, giving 3.49. The tempting shortcut is to read the 4 in the concentration as the answer, but the concentration must pass through a logarithm, and that is what makes pH a logarithmic scale where a tenfold change in hydrogen ions moves the value by exactly one unit. Reporting 0.51 keeps the mantissa and throws the exponent away.
questions.hint: Use pH = -log[H+], and handle the exponent separately.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: connect specific heat capacity to temperature buffering
questions.stem: A large lake warms much more slowly through a spring afternoon than the small puddle beside it, even though both absorb the same sunlight per square metre. Which property of water mainly accounts for that difference?

options.text: Its high specific heat capacity, so a lot of energy is needed per degree
Its high boiling point, which stops solar energy leaving as water vapour
options.misconception: credits the boiling point rather than heat storage per degree

options.text: Its hydrogen bonds, which swallow heat and store it as new bonds
options.misconception: treats breaking hydrogen bonds as the act that absorbs the heat

options.text: Its surface tension, which slows the transfer of heat from air to water
options.misconception: confuses surface tension with the rate of heat exchange

questions.explanation: Specific heat capacity is the energy needed to raise the temperature of one gram by one degree, and water's is among the highest of any common substance, so the same sunlight barely moves its temperature. The lake is slower because it holds vastly more grams of water, not because its surface behaves differently. The tempting belief that hydrogen bonds store the heat is close but reversed: the energy goes into molecular motion as existing bonds break, and a high boiling point limits evaporation rather than warming.
questions.hint: Compare the energy needed per gram per degree of rise.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: explain evaporative cooling using bond breaking and specific heat
questions.stem: A student leaves four identical open beakers in a warm room for 30 minutes: one with 200 millilitres of water, one with 200 millilitres of seawater, one with 200 millilitres of cooking oil, and one with a 200 gram block of metal. The thermocouples show oil warming fastest, metal next, then seawater, and water ending slightly below room temperature. Which set of properties explains that ranking?

options.text: Specific heat per gram plus evaporative loss, which removes the fastest molecules
Boiling points, because a lower boiling point means more stored energy per degree
options.misconception: confuses boiling point with heat capacity per unit mass

options.text: Densities, because a denser sample always absorbs more heat for the same rise
options.misconception: believes density alone determines how fast a sample warms

options.text: Surface tensions, because a higher surface tension traps solar heat in the sample
options.misconception: credits surface tension with controlling heat gain

questions.explanation: Two separate effects set the ranking. Water's high specific heat capacity means each gram needs a lot of energy per degree, and evaporation adds a second effect: the fastest molecules leave the surface carrying away more than their share of the average kinetic energy, so the remaining liquid cools below room temperature. Seawater loses less by evaporation because dissolved solutes lower its vapour pressure, and oil has a far lower specific heat than water. The tempting belief that boiling point sets the ranking confuses the temperature at which a liquid boils with how much energy it absorbs per gram.
questions.hint: Two energy effects are at work: one per gram per degree, one at the surface.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Water: Solubility of Salts and Oils
questions.learningObjective: explain like dissolves like in terms of polarity
questions.stem: Table salt vanishes when stirred into a beaker of water, while olive oil remains a separate layer floating on top. What best explains the difference?

options.text: Water's polarity hydrates the salt's ions but cannot solvate nonpolar oil
The salt is heavier than water while the oil is lighter than water
options.misconception: attributes solubility to density rather than to molecular interactions

options.text: Both dissolve, but the dissolved oil rises afterwards because it is less dense
options.misconception: claims the oil dissolves and then floats, reversing cause and effect

options.text: The salt chemically reacts with the water to form a new dissolved compound
options.misconception: believes dissolving requires a chemical reaction with the solvent

questions.explanation: Sodium chloride is a lattice of cations and anions, and polar water molecules orient their partially negative oxygens toward the sodium and their partially positive hydrogens toward the chloride, pulling the ions out of the lattice and surrounding each one with a hydration shell. Olive oil is a chain of nonpolar C-C and C-H bonds, which offer water nothing to hydrogen-bond to, so the oil molecules cluster together and separate from the water instead. The tempting belief that dissolving means reacting fails because the dissolved species are still sodium and chloride ions, chemically unaltered.
questions.hint: Ask what the solvent and the solute have in common in terms of polarity.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Water: Hydration of a Folded Protein
questions.learningObjective: connect hydration shells to protein solubility
questions.stem: A figure shows a globular protein drawn as a folded ribbon, with small open circles scattered over its outer surface and each circle marked as one water molecule. The circles crowd thickly beside the polar groups of the chain and thin out over the stretches that are mostly carbon and hydrogen. What does that crowding show?

options.text: Water hydrates the polar and charged groups on the protein's outer surface
Water bonds covalently to every surface group and crosslinks the folded chain
options.misconception: promotes hydration hydrogen bonds to full covalent bonds

options.text: Water is repelled by the whole protein and gathers in the surrounding bulk
options.misconception: claims water is excluded from the protein surface everywhere

options.text: Water hydrogen-bonds to the protein and replaces its own internal bonding
options.misconception: believes hydration unfolds the protein by replacing backbone bonds

questions.explanation: The crowding marks hydration: polar side chains and the backbone's carbonyl and amide groups form hydrogen bonds with water, so water packs tightly around them, while nonpolar C-H surfaces exclude water and stay comparatively dry, which is exactly why soluble proteins bury their hydrophobic residues in the core. The tempting belief that hydration crosslinks the fold confuses a solvent interaction with a covalent bond, and water is not repelled by the molecule as a whole, since the protein presents thousands of groups that attract it.
questions.hint: Compare a carbonyl group with a methylene group in the same chain.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Acids and Bases: Buffer pH from a Conjugate Pair
questions.learningObjective: calculate buffer pH from a conjugate pair ratio
questions.stem: A buffer is made from 0.20 molar sodium acetate and 0.10 molar acetic acid, and the acetic acid pKa is 4.75. Using the Henderson-Hasselbalch relation, what is the pH of this buffer to two decimal places?

options.misconception: subtracts the logarithm of the ratio instead of adding it
assumes a buffer always sits exactly at its pKa
doubles the log term by using the ratio the wrong way twice

questions.explanation: The Henderson-Hasselbalch relation states pH equals pKa plus the log of base over acid, so the ratio here is 0.20 over 0.10, which is 2, and log of 2 is 0.30, giving 4.75 plus 0.30, that is 5.05. The tempting belief that a buffer sits at its pKa holds only when the two components are equal in amount, so with twice as much acetate as acid the pH must sit a full 0.30 units above the pKa. Subtracting the log instead of adding it gives 4.45, which is below the pKa the acid itself sets, an impossible position for this mixture.
questions.hint: Compute the ratio first, then take its logarithm.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Acids and Bases: The Bicarbonate Buffer in Blood
questions.learningObjective: explain how carbonic acid and bicarbonate buffer blood
questions.stem: Blood holds its pH near 7.4 even after a meal adds acid and after heavy exercise adds base. Which system does most of that work?

options.text: The carbonic acid and bicarbonate pair, which can shift either way
A high background concentration of free hydroxide ions soaking up acid
options.misconception: blames a high hydroxide concentration instead of the conjugate pair

options.text: A huge store of carbonic acid that soaks up every base entering the blood
options.misconception: credits only the acid half and ignores the bicarbonate half

options.text: A weak acid bound to blood protein that hydrogen ions cannot displace
options.misconception: treats a protein-bound acid as immune to proton displacement

questions.explanation: The buffer pair is carbonic acid and its conjugate base bicarbonate. When acid arrives, bicarbonate binds the protons to become carbonic acid; when base arrives, carbonic acid donates protons to become bicarbonate, and because carbon dioxide can be exhaled the acid side can leave the body entirely. The tempting belief that a large store of acid alone would suffice fails because the partner that removes base is the bicarbonate, and the belief that free hydroxide matters fails because millimolar hydroxide would already destroy blood cells.
questions.hint: Name both partners of the pair, and what each one does.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Acids and Bases: Titration Buffering Region
questions.learningObjective: locate and explain the buffering region on a titration curve
questions.stem: A lab titrates 50 millilitres of 0.10 molar acetic acid with 0.10 molar sodium hydroxide, recording pH after every millilitre. The curve rises slowly at first, then climbs very steeply, then levels off near 8.7 beyond the equivalence point. Which reading of the whole curve is correct?

options.text: The steep jump is the buffer region, where added base is fully consumed
options.misconception: mistakes the steep part of the curve for the buffering region

options.text: The slow rise is the buffer region, and the steep jump marks its exhaustion
Buffering is strongest where acetate is most abundant, just before the endpoint
options.misconception: links capacity to total acetate instead of to the ratio

options.text: The flat tail after the endpoint means all the acetic acid has ionised
options.misconception: reads an excess hydroxide tail as complete acid ionisation

questions.explanation: As hydroxide is added it converts acetic acid into acetate, so for the first stretch both partners are present in useful amounts and the logarithmic relation keeps the pH climbing only slowly: that shallow region is the buffer. Once the acid is nearly exhausted there is nothing left to absorb incoming base, so a tiny addition of hydroxide swings the pH sharply, and past the equivalence point the curve simply tracks the excess hydroxide, which is why the tail flattens near 8.7. The tempting belief that the steep jump is the buffering region inverts the mechanism, because a steep jump is the signature of a buffer running out, and capacity is greatest halfway to the endpoint where the two partners are equal, not where acetate is most abundant.
questions.hint: Ask which partner is still available to absorb incoming base at each point.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: explain why pure water is neutral despite containing ions
questions.stem: Pure water at 25 degrees Celsius is described as neutral even though it contains hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions. What makes it neutral?

options.text: The two ion concentrations are equal at about 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ molar each
There are no ions in pure water until an acid or base is added
options.misconception: believes water is free of ions until something is added to it

options.text: The hydrogen ions stay bound to oxygen and therefore cannot act at all
options.misconception: treats self-ionisation as making the protons chemically inert

options.text: Pure water holds an equal mass of each ion, which is what balances them
options.misconception: confuses equal mass with equal molar concentration for different ions

questions.explanation: Water self-ionises in a very small but exact fraction, splitting a proton from one molecule to another and leaving equal amounts of hydrogen and hydroxide ions at about 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ molar each at 25 degrees, so the net acid or base is zero and the pH is 7. The product of the two concentrations is a fixed constant at a given temperature, which is why adding acid drives the hydroxide side down. The tempting belief that pure water has no ions fails because the slight conductivity of pure water comes entirely from these two ions.
questions.hint: Write out water reacting with itself and count what forms.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Acids and Bases: Why a Buffer Holds pH
questions.learningObjective: explain the equilibrium shift that lets a buffer resist added acid
questions.stem: A solution at pH 7.0 containing equal amounts of a weak acid and its conjugate base receives 0.001 mole of strong acid, and its pH falls only to 6.97. Explain what the conjugate base actually does with those protons.

answer.exemplar: The conjugate base is a proton acceptor, and accepting a proton turns it into the weak acid, a species that is already present in the mixture in similar quantity. The added protons therefore shift the acid-base equilibrium toward the acid side instead of accumulating free, and because pH depends on the logarithm of the ratio of base to acid, moving a partner that already exists in bulk quantity barely changes the value. The tempting wrong belief is that the buffer must be neutralising or destroying the added protons; it is only reassigning them between two partners that differ by one proton, which is exactly why a large enough acid load finally collapses the pH.

questions.explanation: The conjugate base takes protons and becomes the weak acid, so the added hydrogen ions are reassigned rather than removed, and the equilibrium shifts to keep the ratio of base to acid near its starting value. Since pH depends on the logarithm of that ratio, moving a partner that is already present in bulk quantity changes the pH very little, which is why 0.001 mole of strong acid moves this buffer only from 7.0 to 6.97. The tempting belief that the buffer destroys the acid fails because the protons are still there, just carried by the other partner, and that is also why enough acid does collapse the pH.
questions.hint: Follow the fate of one proton, and then consider the size of the shift in the ratio.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: describe a hydrogen bond between water molecules and its strength
questions.stem: Two water molecules approach each other in a beaker. What attraction can form between them, and how strong is it compared with a covalent bond?

options.text: A hydrogen bond to another molecule's oxygen, weaker than a covalent bond
A covalent bond to the other molecule's oxygen, welding the two together
options.misconception: promotes a hydrogen bond to a full covalent bond between molecules

options.text: An ionic bond, since one of the two molecules is negatively charged
options.misconception: labels a polar attraction between uncharged molecules as ionic

options.text: A metallic bond, since the two molecules share a pool of free electrons
options.misconception: mistakes a molecular attraction for a metallic bond

questions.explanation: The partially positive hydrogen of one molecule is attracted to the lone pairs on the partially negative oxygen of another, which is a hydrogen bond: individually weak, a fraction of a covalent bond's strength, but numerous and constantly forming and breaking, which is what gives water its cohesive behaviour. The tempting belief that this is covalent fails because the two molecules keep separate identities and the bond releases energy when broken rather than locking them together permanently, which is why a drop of water is not a rigid lattice like a crystal.
questions.hint: Compare what happens to the two molecules when the interaction breaks.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: relate carbon's four bonds to the shapes carbon skeletons can take
questions.stem: Carbon forms four covalent bonds in almost every organic molecule. What does that single fact make possible?

options.text: Chains, branches and rings, because a bond can join another carbon atom
Only straight chains, because a four-bonded carbon cannot fit a ring
options.misconception: believes four bonds forbid curved or closed structures

options.text: Unlimited bonding, because carbon can exceed four bonds under pressure
options.misconception: assumes the four-bond rule can be broken without limit

options.text: No rings or branches, because every carbon must bond to a hydrogen
options.misconception: thinks every carbon must carry hydrogen rather than carbon

questions.explanation: With four valences to fill, each carbon can bond to other carbons, so the skeleton can be a chain, a branch or a closed ring, and the shape of that skeleton is what gives organic molecules their variety. The tempting belief that four bonds force straight lines fails because the bond angles are about 109.5 degrees rather than 180, so a tetrahedral set of four bonds closes neatly into a ring, as cyclopropane and every sugar ring show.
questions.hint: Recall the bond angle around a carbon with four single bonds.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: explain why carbon-carbon catenation underpins biomolecular variety
questions.stem: Carbon bonds to carbon far more readily than silicon does, a property called catenation. Why does that matter so much to biology?

options.text: Long carbon skeletons can carry many different functional groups at once
Carbon-carbon bonds are the only bonds strong enough to exist in cells
options.misconception: claims only carbon-carbon bonds are stable enough for life

options.text: Long carbon chains store more energy per bond than any other bond
options.misconception: misreads catenation as a statement about bond energy

options.text: Catenation lets carbon dissolve in water more readily than any other atom
options.misconception: confuses catenation with solubility in water

The tempting belief that catenation concerns energy per bond misreads it, because it is about chain length and flexibility, and that is also why silicon, which chains poorly, cannot fill the same structural role.

questions.learningObjective: explain what a carbon-carbon double bond does to chain geometry
questions.stem: A biologist compares a hydrocarbon chain containing one carbon-carbon double bond with a fully saturated chain of the same length. What structural difference does that double bond create?

options.text: A fixed angle and a kink, because the carbons can no longer rotate
A weaker bond, because four shared electrons are less stable than two pairs
options.misconception: believes a double bond is weaker than a single bond

options.text: A permanent charge, because the extra electron pair comes from outside the chain
options.misconception: treats a shared electron pair as a formal charge on carbon

options.text: An extra hydrogen, because the double bond pulls one from the surrounding water
options.misconception: thinks a double bond strips hydrogen from nearby molecules

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Carbon: Bonds to Nitrogen, Oxygen, Sulfur and Phosphorus
questions.learningObjective: relate electronegativity differences to functional group reactivity
questions.stem: Carbon bonds not only to itself but also to oxygen, nitrogen, sulfur and phosphorus. Why does that single fact generate most of the chemical behaviour seen in cells?

options.text: Those atoms differ in electronegativity, so the groups they form are polar and reactive
Those atoms are larger than carbon, so they bend the skeleton into fixed shapes
options.misconception: attributes group reactivity to the size of the attached atom

options.text: Those atoms are rarer in the environment, so organisms must conserve them
options.misconception: invents a conservation reason for a bonding fact

options.text: Those atoms form weaker bonds, so the molecule breaks apart more easily
options.misconception: confuses polarity-driven reactivity with weak bonding

questions.explanation: Because oxygen and nitrogen pull shared electrons harder than carbon does, the hydroxyl, carboxyl, amino and phosphate groups they form carry partial charges, and those charges are what let the groups act as donors, acceptors and links to other molecules; the same carbon skeleton becomes a sugar, an amino acid or a nucleotide depending on which groups hang off it. The tempting belief that these bonds are weak is backwards, since C-O and C-N bonds are strong, and it is their polarity, not their weakness, that makes the groups chemically active.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the shared electrons when oxygen is one partner.

questions.topic: Acids and Bases: Proton Donors and Acceptors
questions.learningObjective: assign acid and base roles in a proton transfer step
questions.stem: In the step where bicarbonate accepts a hydrogen ion and becomes carbonic acid, what role does each of the two species play?

options.text: Bicarbonate is the proton acceptor, the base; carbonic acid is its conjugate acid
Bicarbonate is the proton donor, the acid; carbonic acid is the conjugate base
options.misconception: reverses donor and acceptor in a proton transfer

options.text: Both are acids, since each can release a hydrogen ion in another step
options.misconception: insists both partners share one label in a given step

options.text: The roles depend on the solvent, so neither can be labelled here
options.misconception: believes acid and base labels are undefined away from water

The tempting belief that both partners must share one label fails because accepting and donating are different jobs, and the labels are not at the mercy of the solvent, since the pair still differs by exactly one proton wherever the reaction runs.

questions.learningObjective: identify functional groups from a described structure
questions.stem: A figure shows a two-carbon skeleton. The left carbon is drawn with a hydrogen, with an oxygen that carries its own hydrogen, and with the bond to the other carbon. The right carbon is drawn double-bonded to an oxygen and single-bonded to a hydrogen. Which functional groups does this molecule contain?

options.text: A hydroxyl group and a carboxyl group on the two-carbon skeleton
An amino group and a hydroxyl group on the two-carbon skeleton
options.misconception: reads a carbon bonded to oxygen as carrying an amino group

options.text: A phosphate group and a carboxyl group on the two-carbon skeleton
options.misconception: sees a double-bonded oxygen and assumes a phosphate group

options.text: An amine group and a hydroxyl group on the two-carbon skeleton
options.misconception: confuses a carboxylic acid with a hydroxyl-bearing amine

questions.explanation: The left carbon bears an oxygen bonded to a hydrogen, which is a hydroxyl group, and the right carbon bears a carbon double-bonded to an oxygen, which together with that same hydroxyl makes a carboxyl group, so the molecule is an organic acid. The tempting belief that an amine is present fails because nitrogen appears nowhere in the drawn structure, and a phosphate group needs a phosphorus at its centre, which this molecule does not contain.
questions.hint: Count the heteroatoms in the drawing, then group them.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: explain why a shared molecular formula does not identify a substance
questions.stem: A student finds two organic molecules, both listed with the molecular formula C6H12O6, and concludes they must be the same substance because the element counts match. What is the flaw in that conclusion?

options.text: A shared formula does not fix how the atoms are bonded to each other
The formula must also record the physical phase of the sample
options.misconception: thinks phase data is what a molecular formula must record

options.text: Matching element counts can still leave the two molar masses different
options.misconception: believes isomer pairs must differ in molar mass

options.text: A molecular formula must list every bond before a substance is named
options.misconception: confuses a molecular formula with a full structural diagram

questions.explanation: A molecular formula counts atoms without saying how they are joined, and the arrangement is what decides melting point, enzyme recognition and reactivity, so C6H12O6 covers glucose and fructose and other isomers with different properties. The tempting belief that the formula must be expanded into a full structural drawing is backwards, because the formula is the summary and the structure is the extra information it leaves out. Isomers also share molar mass exactly, so mass cannot break the tie.
questions.hint: Ask what the formula does not record about the bonds.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Water: Hydrophobic Skeletons and Hydrophilic Groups
questions.learningObjective: contrast a nonpolar carbon skeleton with polar functional groups in water
questions.stem: One lipid is described as having a long hydrocarbon tail with a single small polar head group, while a sugar carries five hydroxyl groups. Why does the lipid separate from water while the sugar dissolves?

options.text: The C-C and C-H bonds are nonpolar, so water cannot hydrogen-bond to the tail
The tail is negatively charged, so it repels the polar water molecules
options.misconception: treats a nonpolar hydrocarbon tail as formally charged

options.text: The tail is shorter than the head, so the molecule is too small to dissolve
options.misconception: explains insolubility by size instead of by polarity

options.text: The tail is made of protein, which water digests into soluble pieces
options.misconception: confuses a hydrocarbon chain with a protein chain

questions.explanation: Water's hydrogen bonds are the only attractions strong enough to pull molecules into solution, and C-C and C-H bonds are nonpolar, so the tail offers water nothing to bond to while the water molecules bond to each other around it, which is why lipids separate out. Sugars are the opposite case, because several hydroxyl groups each donate and accept hydrogen bonds. The tempting belief that a nonpolar chain is charged confuses polar, which means uneven charge distribution, with charged.
questions.hint: Ask which intermolecular attraction the tail can take part in.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: predict the direction of osmotic flow and the resulting level change
questions.stem: A figure shows two beakers side by side, each holding 100 millilitres of liquid, separated by a clay wall that water passes through but sucrose does not. The left beaker holds pure water and its level is lower, while the right beaker holds 0.20 molar sucrose and its level is higher, with the wall bowed towards the left. In which direction does the net flow of water occur, and what does that flow do to the volumes?

options.text: From the dilute side to the concentrated side, adding volume on the right
From the concentrated side to the dilute side, removing volume from the right
options.misconception: reverses the direction of osmotic flow

options.text: From the concentrated side to the dilute side, adding volume on the left
options.misconception: pairs the right direction of flow with the wrong outcome

options.text: No net flow occurs, since the two levels already sit at different heights
options.misconception: treats unequal levels as proof that net flow has stopped

questions.explanation: Water crosses the wall by osmosis, moving so that the solute concentration on both sides equalises, so net flow runs from lower solute concentration to higher and the pure water side gains volume while the sucrose side loses it, which is exactly the level difference drawn. The tempting belief that water always flows toward pure water confuses a gradient in solute with a gradient in water, and the claim of no net flow is wrong because the two sides started unequal, so equilibrium cannot already be established.
questions.hint: Follow the solute gradient, not the direction of the name.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Water: Preparing a Solution of Known Molarity
questions.learningObjective: convert molarity and volume into a mass of solute
questions.stem: A technician needs 250 millilitres of a 0.40 molar glucose solution for a culture plate, and glucose has a molar mass of 180 grams per mole. How many grams of glucose should be weighed out?

options.misconception: drops the molarity factor and uses the volume alone
ignores the 0.250 litre volume and multiplies by molar mass
shifts the decimal place on the mole count before multiplying

questions.explanation: Molarity is moles per litre, so 0.250 litres of a 0.40 molar solution contains 0.40 times 0.250, which is 0.100 mole, and multiplying by 180 grams per mole gives 18 grams. The tempting shortcut of multiplying the molarity straight by the molar mass gives 72 grams and pretends a whole litre was made. The trap of treating 0.40 as a mass fraction gives a different kind of number entirely, because the molarity has to be converted to moles before the molar mass is applied.
questions.hint: Convert the volume to litres, then find the moles, then the grams.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Acids and Bases: Hydrogen Ions in a Volume
questions.learningObjective: convert a pH into an amount of hydrogen ions in a stated volume
questions.practice: quantity calculation with a logarithmic step
questions.stem: A sample of rainwater has a pH of 4.00. How many moles of hydrogen ions are present in 3.0 litres of that water, reported to two significant figures?

options.misconception: reports the pure water ion concentration, not the acid present
stops at the concentration and skips the volume
shifts the decimal on the concentration by one power of ten

questions.explanation: A pH of 4.00 corresponds to a hydrogen ion concentration of 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ molar, because pH is the negative logarithm of that concentration. Multiplying by the 3.0 litre volume then gives 3.0 × 10⁻⁴ mole. The tempting belief that the answer is the concentration itself answers a different question, and 3.0 × 10⁻⁷ mole is the ion content of pure water, not the acid that the low pH records.
questions.hint: Turn the pH back into a concentration before multiplying by the volume.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: explain how water both joins and splits subunits by the same chemistry
questions.stem: A cell joins glucose units into a starch grain, and later a digestive enzyme splits a protein into peptides. Explain how the same small molecule, water, both joins subunits and cuts them apart.

answer.exemplar: Both directions run on the same covalent chemistry. In condensation, a hydroxyl from one substrate and a hydrogen from another leave together as a water molecule, which forms the ester or amide bond between the two subunits and releases energy the cell can capture. In hydrolysis, a water molecule is split across that bond, its hydroxyl going to one fragment and its hydrogen to the other, restoring the exact functional groups the subunits had before they were joined. Since the pair of reactions is reversible, an enzyme can drive it either way by shifting the water concentration or by coupling it to an energy source. The tempting wrong belief is that water is only a passive solvent here, when water is a reactant in one direction and a product in the other.

questions.explanation: The two processes are the same chemistry run in opposite directions: condensation removes one hydroxyl and one hydrogen as water, which is how a bond between two subunits forms, while hydrolysis puts that same water back across the bond, restoring the hydroxyl and hydrogen the subunits carried before they were joined. Because the pair is reversible, an enzyme can drive it either way by shifting the water concentration or by coupling it to an energy source, which is why one cell can both store starch and digest protein. The tempting belief that water is only a solvent fails because water is consumed and released in these reactions.
questions.hint: Track the hydroxyl group and the hydrogen in each direction.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Water: Floating Ice and Lake Stratification
questions.learningObjective: evaluate a claim about lake cooling using the density maximum of water
questions.stem: A student argues that because ice floats, a lake must cool uniformly to 4 degrees Celsius before any of it freezes. Why is that reasoning wrong?

options.text: Water is densest at 4 degrees, so the surface reaches 0 last and freezes there
Ice floats only in fresh water, so lakes never freeze from the top down
options.misconception: denies top-down freezing by applying salt-water behaviour

options.text: A lake can only reach 4 degrees after ice has already sealed the top
options.misconception: reverses the order, putting ice formation before density mixing

options.text: Water is densest at 0 degrees, so the coldest water stays on the surface
options.misconception: believes maximum density coincides with the freezing point

questions.explanation: The flaw is the assumed uniform cooling. Fresh water reaches its maximum density at 4 degrees Celsius, so water at that temperature sinks while water colder than 4 degrees stays on top, and the surface, in contact with cold air, is the last region to reach 0 and the place where ice appears. Floating ice then insulates the water below, so a shallow pond can freeze solid while a deep lake keeps liquid beneath the cap. The tempting belief that the densest water is the coldest confuses maximum density with the freezing point.
questions.hint: Separate the density maximum from the freezing point, then follow the circulation.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Acids and Bases: Choosing a Buffer from Data
questions.learningObjective: judge buffering capacity from a fixed acid load and justify the choice
questions.stem: Four solutions, each starting at pH 7.0, are tested by adding 1 millilitre of 1 molar hydrochloric acid to each. Sample A falls to pH 4.0, sample B to 5.0, sample C to 6.0 and sample D to 6.9. Which sample is the better buffer for this acid load, and what does the comparison establish?

options.text: Sample D, because its pH moved least once the acid was added
Sample A, because it reacted most, showing it absorbed the most acid
options.misconception: mistakes the largest pH fall for the best buffering performance

options.text: Sample C, since a buffer must show a clear drop to prove it is working
options.misconception: assumes a working buffer must show a visible pH fall

options.text: Sample B, because a buffer resists acid and alkali equally at once
options.misconception: assumes perfect symmetry between resistance to acid and base

questions.explanation: Buffering capacity is judged by how little the pH moves under a fixed acid load, and sample D's shift of 0.1 unit against 3.0 units for sample A shows it had the most proton-accepting partner available relative to the acid added. Sample A behaved as an unbuffered solution does, which is why its large fall is evidence against it rather than for it. The tempting belief that a buffer resists acid and alkali equally fails because resistance to base depends on how much of the acid partner is present, which is a separate quantity from the base available for protons.
questions.hint: Rank the samples by the size of the pH change, smallest first.
